title: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, vol. 2 (Kimmei, 13th year)
venue: Transactions and Proceedings of the Japan Society, London, Supplement I (Internet Archive scan)
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: My law shall spread to the East
summary: Kimmei 13th year, winter 10th month (Aston prints the year as A.D. 552): King Syeng-myeng of Pekche sends a gold-and-copper Shaka image, flags, umbrellas and sutras, with a memorial praising the doctrine; Soga no Iname is allowed to try the cult, a pestilence follows, and the image is thrown into the Naniha canal.
limits: The passage states a Pekche-to-Yamato transfer of Buddhism, but it is an 8th-century court narrative and its date and wording are disputed (see Yoshida 2003). Quoted from Aston's 1896 English translation through OCR text; the original is Classical Chinese. Aston's own note says Buddhism reached Koguryo in 372 and Pekche in 384.

strand.what: Buddhist image and sutras sent by King Seong, with a memorial

text.locator: Book XIX, Kimmei, 13th year (Aston vol. 2, pp. 65-67)
text.edition: Aston, Nihongi, Japan Society London 1896, via Internet Archive nihongi2asto

composition.basis: Yoshida 2003, JJRS 30/1-2 (opened): 'the Nihon shoki compiled in 720'; the 552 date itself is judged not a historical fact in the same article

text.witness: Not established from sources opened; earliest manuscripts not checked

title: Revisioning Religion in Ancient Japan
venue: Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 30/1-2: 1-26
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: was not translated into Chinese until 703
summary: Argues that the Nihon shoki's Kimmei passage cites a Golden Light Sutra version not translated into Chinese until 703, that 552 was chosen from a mappo calculation, and that 538 (Gangoji engi, Jogu Shotoku hootei setsu) is a later hypothesis; 'we have no basis for pinning down a specific date', only that the Paekche-to-Kinmei story circulated from the late 7th to 8th century.
limits: Expert reassessment, not a neutral survey; it rejects both traditional dates rather than choosing one. Text is OCR of a PDF with spacing errors. Concerns the date and the narrative, not whether Buddhism came from Paekche (it accepts transmission around the mid-6th century).

strand.what: Buddhism, with the traditional 552 and 538 dates both rejected as historical facts

title: The Credibility of the Gangoji engi
venue: Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 42/1: 89-107
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: should be considered a forgery from a later period
summary: Shows the Gangoji garan engi, the main source for the 538 date of Buddhism's arrival, claims composition in 747 but is probably a late 9th-century and later compilation.
limits: Bears on the 538 date only through that text; the article is about one document's credibility.

strand.what: The 538 date for Buddhist transmission rests on a text judged a later forgery

title: Nihongi vol. 2 (Suiko, 18th year): the Koguryo priest Tam-chhi
venue: Transactions and Proceedings of the Japan Society, London, Supplement I (Internet Archive scan)
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: skilled in preparing painters' colours, paper, and ink
summary: Suiko 18th year (Aston places it in 610): Koguryo sends priests Tam-chhi (Damjing) and Pop-chong; Tam-chhi knew the five Chinese classics, prepared colours, paper and ink, and made mills.
limits: Aston's rendering says the priest was skilled in preparing paper; whether this is the first paper in Japan is not stated by the passage and is disputed by later readers. Retrospective 720 compilation reporting a 610 event.

strand.what: Paper, ink, pigment and millstone making, and Confucian classics, brought by a Buddhist priest

title: Nihongi vol. 1, Introduction (Writing)
venue: Transactions and Proceedings of the Japan Society, London, Supplement I (Internet Archive scan)
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: The date of its first introduction is not definitely known
summary: Aston states that the first positive information on Chinese writing in Japan belongs to A.D. 405, for which the Nihongi gives an erroneous date corresponding to A.D. 285; Wani (Wang-in) of Korea was tutor to an imperial prince, and Korea was the intermediary by which China became known to Japan.
limits: A scholar of 1896, now dated; useful as the translator's own chronology caution (a 120-year cycle error), not as modern consensus.

title: Kojiki, Preface (Yasumaro's memorial)
venue: Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan, Supplement (English Wikisource transcription)
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: it would be difficult to arrange phrases and compose periods in the characters
summary: Yasumaro explains that, ordered in 711 (Wado 4) to record Hieda no Are's oral tradition, he wrote with Chinese characters used sometimes by sound and sometimes by sense because archaic Japanese was hard to fit to them; the memorial is dated the 28th day of the 1st month of Wado 5.
limits: The preface's own dating (712 per Chamberlain's note and Wikipedia) is internal evidence; a few scholars have doubted the preface, which was not examined here. Chamberlain's translation is 19th century.

strand.what: Chinese characters adapted to record Japanese by phonetic and ideographic use

title: Samguk sagi, vol. 18, Goguryeo annals 6: King Sosurim, year 2
venue: Chinese Wikisource transcription of Samguk sagi (juan 18)
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: 遣使及浮屠順道，送佛像、經文
summary: Sosurim year 2, 6th month (372 by standard reckoning): Fu Jian of Former Qin sends envoys and the monk Sundo (Shun Dao) with Buddha images and scriptures; the king founds a Taehak (academy) to teach youth; year 5 founds Seongmun temple for Sundo and Ibullan for Ado, 'the beginning of Buddhism in Haedong'.
limits: Samguk sagi is a 12th-century compilation about events up to 800 years earlier; years here are the work's own regnal reckoning. Transcription includes editorial footnote markers.

title: Hunminjeongeum (Haerye edition), preface
venue: Korean Wikisource transcription of the Haerye edition
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: 國之語音。異乎中國。與文字不相流通
summary: Sejong's preface says the sounds of Korean differ from China's and do not fit Chinese characters, so the common people cannot express themselves; he made 28 letters. The postface is dated 正統十一年九月上澣, the first ten days of the 9th month of Zhengtong 11 (1446).
limits: Documents Korean rejection and adaptation of an imported script rather than its arrival. The wikisource transcription's variant characters and notes were not independently collated.

title: Bibliographical Characteristics of the Movable Metal Type and Woodblock-printed Jikji and Quotations from Venerable Baegun
venue: Review of Korean Studies 29(1): 351-
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
quote: 宣光七年丁巳七月日淸州牧外興德寺鑄字印施

title: Hou Hanshu 76 (Xunli liezhuan): Xi Guang and Ren Yan in Jiaozhi and Jiuzhen

ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

summary: Xi Guang, grand administrator of Jiaozhi under Emperor Ping, 'taught the people and barbarians, gradually through rites and righteousness'; Ren Yan in Jiuzhen taught ploughing with iron tools and marriage rites; 'Chinese customs in Lingnan began with these two governors'.
limits: Written some centuries after the events (Wikipedia: completed over two hundred years after the fall of the Han). Moralising Han-official narrative; says nothing of Vietnamese response. Wikipedia date not independently checked against Fan Ye's life.

title: Hanji used as art materials: historical consideration
authors: Lee J.-Y.; Kim C.-H.; et al.
venue: KFS Journal 20(3): 191-197 (as printed on the PDF header)
ask_addressed: East Asia: how Chinese writing, Buddhism, Confucian learning and technologies reached Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

summary: States Chinese paper reached Korea by trade in Sosurim's reign, that it is not certain when papermaking itself was introduced, and that tradition places papermaking in Korea well before the 7th century.

title: Choe Museon (encyclopedia article)

limits: Rebuts one Needham claim (the matchlock), not his gunpowder thesis, and the quotation is garbled by the two-column PDF layout; the sentence it completes is about Needham's matchlock origin. Outside the Korea-Japan-Vietnam core.
